Hey, morning, Haslinda. So at this point, this is actually a fairly significant change. As
you just outlined, under the current rules for these F&J visas, I will point out there's
about 1.5 million students that are in the United States on these types of visas. They're
allowed to stay sort of as long as their studies last. It's very different from other forms
of non-immigrant visas in the United States. And so as long as they're enrolled in sort
of the minimum number of credits that they need at these universities, they can stay. Under
this new rule, though, as you just mentioned, this imposes a four-year limit. Before then,
if they need to stay in the United States for longer to continue their studies, they
actually have to go and seek more duration of time. They have to seek an extension,
provide some biometric data, and basically, it's sort of handled this in a way where
previously maybe their universities would have helped coordinate this. But again,
this doesn't pose a pretty significant barrier here. So very, very, very different change.
It's a different change. Who is it likely to hit the worst? I mean, we know that lots
of Chinese and Indian students in the US. Yes, exactly right. So I would expect this
